newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian coffee head Cardenas praises ACPC unity. [CORRECTED 22:37 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Colombian coffee head Cardenas praises ACPC unity. [CORRECTED 22:37 GMT]

text.p: The managing direcor of Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation praised the Association of Coffee Producing Countries Tuesday, saying its export retention plan had led to a "substantial reduction" in consumer stocks and demonstrated unprecedented unity among the world's top coffee-growing countries.

"It hasn't been easy to make an instrument of this nature work," said Jorge Cardenas, in reference ot the ACPC retention plan. "But the countries have been growing accustomed to it and are showing the necessary political will to consolidate the process."
The ACPC agreed last May to limit green coffee exports from its members to 53.5 million 60-kilo bags in the year to June 1997 against 45.8 million in the previous 12 months.

Cardenas, who spoke in an annual address to the National Coffee Growers' Congress in Bogota, said this had led to a "substantial reduction in the inventories in the hands of importing countries" and that this in turn had produced "salutary effects on international prices."
More importantly, however, he said the ACPC had demonstrated "consensus and unity" among leading producer countries "in contrast with the divisions that prevailed in the past."

Cardenas was clearly referring to the political infighting and cheating on export quotas -- including by Colombia -- that led to the collapse of efforts to build a new International Coffee Agreement in 1993 when the United States announced that it was pulling out of the International Coffee Organization. (Corrects to indicate that the ICA had already fallen apart prior to September 1993.)
Despite Cardenas's upbeat assessment, diplomats and international coffee experts remain skeptical about the long term success of the ACPC retention plan.
One Bogota-based diplomat, who asked not be identified, said the only way to ensure the plan worked would be to burn all stockpiles in producer countries beyond their assigned quotas.
